idiom_name: contract unit + implementation unit + composition root
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create a unit that contains only the contract (operations, signatures, semantics, error model) and that both sides may depend on; implement it in a unit the client never references, and bind the two at a single composition root (factory, registry, container, service loader). Keep the contract expressed in domain terms and free of implementation types so the contract unit stays deployable wherever the implementation cannot go. Where the runtime offers structural typing the consumer may declare the contract itself; where it does not, the contract unit is a shared artifact that needs an explicit versioning policy.
code_sketch:
contract/   interface Clock { now(): Instant }
impl/       class SystemClock implements Clock
main/       clock = factory.create(Clock.class); new Report(clock)
# contract/ alone is deployed to clients that cannot load impl/
pitfalls: The composition root is the only place allowed to know both sides; letting clients construct implementations recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
A contract that grows implementation-specific members silently re-couples the client to the implementation.
Without a versioning policy the contract unit becomes the most expensive artifact to change.
If the contract unit itself depends on infrastructure or implementation packages, clients pull the implementation in transitively and the dependency arrow never actually inverts.

Copying the contract file into the client tree and the implementation tree instead of shipping one shared artifact: the two copies drift and the mismatch surfaces at link, deployment or ABI load time, not at compile time.

Moving implementation conveniences (base classes, configuration, shared utilities) into the contract unit to 'help' implementors: the contract becomes heavier than the implementation and every helper becomes published API that consumers and third parties inherit.
